note: Industry-standard practice, written once and reused. This is GENERAL knowledge, never the candidate's own experience: the writer may use it as the backbone of a 'how I would' answer, and must not claim the candidate did it. Edit freely; ids are stable keys.

practices.title: Designing long-term memory for an agent that works with a business over months
practices.body:
Split memory by purpose, not into one big transcript. (1) Working memory: the current task and recent turns inside the context window. (2) Episodic memory: a timestamped log of interactions, decisions and their outcomes, stored as rolling summaries plus the raw events behind them. (3) Semantic memory: durable facts about the business (products, customers, policies, preferences, constraints) kept as structured records with a source, a timestamp and a confidence. (4) Procedural memory: how this business wants things done (approved workflows, templates, escalation rules).
Writing: extract candidate facts from each conversation, deduplicate against existing records, and resolve conflicts explicitly (the newer fact supersedes the old one, the old one is kept as history with an audit trail; critical facts such as pricing or compliance rules need human confirmation before they are trusted). Add expiry or review dates to facts that go stale.
Reading: retrieve rather than stuff. Hybrid search (vector plus keyword plus metadata filters for entity, date and type), then re-rank by relevance, recency and importance, and inject only the few records the task needs, each with its source so answers can cite it. Compact old episodes into summaries on a schedule.
Safety and operations: isolate memory per business (tenant), treat personal data carefully with retention and deletion paths, never let the model write directly to the durable store without validation, and monitor memory quality (recall of known facts after months, contradiction rate, stale-fact rate).

practices.title: Evaluating whether an LLM, RAG or agent system actually improved
practices.body:
Build the test set first: a labelled golden set of real or realistic cases (roughly 50 to 200 to start), stratified by difficulty and by the failure modes that matter, with held-out cases the team never tunes against. Freeze it and version it.
Measure each layer separately. Retrieval: recall@k, precision@k, MRR or nDCG against labelled relevant passages. Generation: faithfulness (is every claim supported by the retrieved context), answer correctness against a reference, and relevance. Agent: task success rate, correct tool selection and arguments, number of steps, latency and cost per task. Use programmatic checks wherever possible (exact match, schema validity, rule checks) and use an LLM judge only for what cannot be checked mechanically, after calibrating the judge against human labels on a sample.
Compare changes properly: run old and new versions on the same set, report paired differences with confidence intervals rather than a single average, and read the failures, not only the score. Run the suite automatically on every prompt, model or retrieval change so regressions are caught before release.
Then confirm online: staged rollout or A/B test with user-facing signals (task completion, escalation or hand-off rate, user corrections, thumbs feedback) and keep sampling real traffic into the golden set.

practices.title: Debugging a RAG system with high retrieval recall but poor answer quality
practices.body:
High recall only says the right passage is somewhere in the retrieved set. Start with error analysis: sample 30 to 50 bad answers and label each failure by type before changing anything. Typical causes, in the order worth checking: low precision (the right chunk is buried among noisy ones, so add re-ranking and tighten top-k), context assembly problems (chunk boundaries that split the answer, duplicates, ordering and truncation so the key passage sits in the middle of a long prompt), the generator ignoring or contradicting the context (check faithfulness, tighten instructions, require citations), query problems (ambiguous or multi-part questions that need rewriting or decomposition), and stale or conflicting source documents.
Fix the most frequent category first, change one thing at a time, and re-run the same labelled set to confirm the metric moved (context precision, faithfulness and answer correctness, not recall).

practices.title: Turning a promising agent prototype into a dependable product
practices.body:
Define what dependable means in measurable terms first (task success rate, error rate, latency and cost per task) and build the evaluation set before polishing anything.
Priorities in order: evaluation and regression tests on every change; guardrails (schema-validated outputs, tool-call validation, permissions and limits on what the agent can do, human approval for irreversible actions); failure handling (timeouts, retries with backoff, fallbacks to a simpler path or a human hand-off when confidence is low, idempotent actions); observability (a full trace of each run: prompts, tool calls, costs, outcomes) with alerts on drift; latency and cost (caching, smaller models for simple steps, parallel tool calls, streaming); UX (show what the agent is doing and why, let the user correct it, make failure states clear). Roll out gradually (shadow mode, then a small share of traffic) and feed real failures back into the evaluation set.

practices.title: An agent produces technically valid results, but users abandon the workflow
practices.body:
Technically correct is not the same as useful, so find where and why users leave before changing the model. Instrument the workflow (where in the flow people stop, time to first useful result, how often they edit or discard the output, completion rate) and pair the numbers with a handful of user conversations or session recordings.
Common causes: the result is correct but arrives too slowly, or in a form the user cannot act on; users cannot see why the agent did something so they do not trust it; the agent asks too much or too little; errors are silent or confusing; the workflow does not fit how the person already works. Fix the largest cause first: show reasoning and sources, make the output editable, cut steps, add sensible defaults, and give an easy way to hand off to a person. Then re-measure the same completion and edit-rate metrics.
